lead: A quantum circuit with n Hadamards can present all 2ⁿ inputs to a function in one oracle call. Measurement still returns one input, not the whole table. Phase kickback supplies the rest: set the target to |−⟩ and each f(x) becomes a sign (−1)ᶠ⁽ˣ⁾ on the matching input state. The signs stay invisible until interference turns them into probabilities. Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon, Grover and phase estimation all rest on this pair of ideas.
prereq: You need: superposition and measurement (Unit 2, Qubits, Postulates and Entanglement), the Hadamard and CNOT gates and the circuit model (Unit 3, Quantum Gates and Circuits), and the reversible oracle used in 4.2.

sections.h3: Quantum parallelism: all inputs in one call

blocks.text: A classical program that wants f on every n-bit input must call f about 2ⁿ times. A quantum circuit prepares all inputs at once with n Hadamard gates and one oracle call.

blocks.where: n = number of input qubits; |0<sup>n</sup>⟩ = all-zero state on those qubits; H<sup>⊗n</sup> = one Hadamard on each qubit; the sum runs over all 2ⁿ bit strings x; each input has amplitude 1/√(2<sup>n</sup>).

blocks.text: With one ancilla in |0⟩, one call of Uf gives (1/√(2n)) Σx |x⟩|f(x)⟩. This is quantum parallelism: f is evaluated at every input in one pass. The amplitude on each |x⟩|f(x)⟩ is physically present, and the registers are entangled when f is not constant.

Measurement ruins it. Reading the first register returns one string x with probability 1/2ⁿ, and the second shows f(x). One call yields one table line. Testing all 2ⁿ inputs this way needs 2ⁿ runs, no better than classical. Useful algorithms do not measure here.

sections.h3: The oracle U<sub>f</sub> and why it needs two registers

blocks.text: The oracle is a unitary gate that computes f reversibly. It reads an n-bit input x and a one-bit target y, and XORs the answer into the target.

blocks.where: x = n-bit input string; y = one ancilla bit, 0 or 1; f(x) ∈ {0,1}; ⊕ = XOR (addition mod 2). Since y ⊕ f(x) ⊕ f(x) = y, U<sub>f</sub> is its own inverse, so the computation is reversible. U<sub>f</sub> maps each basis state |x⟩|y⟩ to another basis state and never merges two, so it is a permutation of the basis; a permutation matrix is unitary, hence U<sub>f</sub> is a valid quantum gate.

blocks.text: An n-bit input usually needs extra workspace qubits inside the oracle. They start in |0⟩, end in |0⟩ and are ignored outside.
The table is parity on n = 2 inputs, used again in the worked example. f is added into the target, never written over it; that is what keeps the gate reversible.

sections.h3: Phase kickback: moving f(x) into a sign

blocks.text: Set the ancilla to |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 and run the same oracle. Because |−⟩ is a superposition, both XOR branches occur.

items: Write the ancilla as (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 and apply U<sub>f</sub> to |x⟩|−⟩.
XOR adds f(x) to each branch: (|x⟩|f(x)⟩ − |x⟩|1⊕f(x)⟩)/√2.

blocks.where: (−1)f(x) = +1 when f(x)=0 and −1 when f(x)=1; the ancilla comes out unchanged. Its phase was kicked back onto the input register, hence phase kickback (some syllabi write phase kick-back).

blocks.text: With the input in uniform superposition the oracle applies every f value at once as signs: U<sub>f</sub>(1/√(2<sup>n</sup>)) Σ<sub>x</sub>|x⟩|−⟩ = (1/√(2<sup>n</sup>)) Σ<sub>x</sub>(−1)<sup>f(x)</sup>|x⟩|−⟩. The ancilla can then be dropped; what matters is the signed superposition of inputs.

A −1 in front of the whole state is a global phase: |ψ⟩ and −|ψ⟩ are the same physical state and no measurement separates them. A sign that differs between basis states is a relative phase; it changes interference and is measurable. Kickback gives a relative phase whenever f takes both 0 and 1. If f is constant, all signs are equal, the factor is global and unobservable, so constant versus balanced needs interference. Measuring now still gives x with probability 1/2ⁿ, so nothing is visible. The signs pay off only after a further gate layer, usually a second Hadamard, turns them into unequal amplitudes.

Phase kickback drives the algorithms that follow. 4.2 uses it so interference reads out f(0)⊕f(1). 4.3 turns signs of a hidden dot product into a measurable string. Grover (4.7) uses the same trick with an f that marks one item. Phase estimation (4.5) is the general form: an eigenstate of a unitary collects its eigenvalue as a phase, and the QFT (4.4) reads it out.

figure.caption: The ancilla |−⟩ stays unchanged; the parity oracle turns f(x) into the signs +1, −1, −1, +1 on |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. The final amplitudes are +1/2, −1/2, −1/2, +1/2.

spec.title: Worked example: n = 2, f = x₁⊕x₂
spec.aria: A table of the four two-bit inputs |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ with parity f(x) = 0, 1, 1, 0, kickback signs +1, −1, −1, +1, final amplitudes ±1/2, and the ancilla unchanged as |−⟩.

examples.question: Take n = 2 input qubits, the parity function f(x) = x₁⊕x₂ where x = x₁x₂, the ancilla in |−⟩, and the input register starting as |00⟩. Apply H to each input qubit, then one call of U_f. Write the state after each stage and give the sign in front of each of the four input basis states.
steps: Start: input |00⟩, ancilla |−⟩ = (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, so the joint state is |00⟩|−⟩.
Hadamards: 1/√4 = 1/2, so H on both qubits gives (1/2)(|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)|−⟩.
Final joint state: (1/2)(|00⟩−|01⟩−|10⟩+|11⟩)|−⟩. The ancilla stays |−⟩ because it is an eigenstate of U_f with eigenvalue (−1)ᶠ⁽ˣ⁾.
Check the norm: (1/2)²×4 = 1, so probabilities are still 1/4 each.
examples.check:
xs = [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]
signs = [(-1) ** (x1 ^ x2) for x1, x2 in xs]
for s in signs:
    print(s)

traps: Thinking one call lets you read f(0), f(1), … by measuring. Measurement collapses to one x; every useful algorithm interferes before measuring.
Using |0⟩ as ancilla and expecting a sign. With |0⟩ the result is |x⟩|f(x)⟩ — a bit in the second register, no relative phase. Kickback needs |−⟩.
Confusing global and relative phase. A single −1 on the whole state is unobservable; the useful sign differs between basis states.
Saying kickback changes the ancilla. |−⟩ is an eigenstate, so it comes out unchanged; only a phase attaches to |x⟩.
Overwriting instead of XOR: U<sub>f</sub>|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|f(x)⟩ is not reversible for general f. Examiners look for ⊕.

quiz.q: Write the state produced by H<sup>⊗n</sup> acting on |0<sup>n</sup>⟩ and name it.
quiz.a: H<sup>⊗n</sup>|0<sup>n</sup>⟩ = (1/√(2<sup>n</sup>)) Σ<sub>x</sub>|x⟩, the uniform superposition of all 2ⁿ strings, each with amplitude 1/√(2<sup>n</sup>).

quiz.q: Define the oracle U<sub>f</sub> on two registers and say why the second register is needed.
quiz.a: U<sub>f</sub>|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩. The second register keeps the gate reversible: XOR can be undone; overwriting cannot.

quiz.q: After H<sup>⊗n</sup> and one U<sub>f</sub> call, the first register holds every f(x). Why does measuring it not give the whole truth table of f?
quiz.a: Measurement collapses to one |x⟩|f(x)⟩, x uniform with probability 1/2ⁿ. One run gives one pair. The rest sits in relative amplitudes and is usable only after interference creates unequal probabilities.

quiz.q: Why does the ancilla remain in |−⟩ during phase kickback, and what goes wrong if it starts in |0⟩?
quiz.a: |−⟩ is an eigenstate of U<sub>f</sub> for every x with eigenvalue (−1)ᶠ⁽ˣ⁾, so it is unchanged and only a phase is picked up. Starting in |0⟩ gives |x⟩|f(x)⟩: the value lands as a bit, no relative phase appears, and no interference can use it.

quiz.q: Let n = 2 and f(x) = x₁, the first bit of x = x₁x₂. Start from |00⟩|−⟩, apply H to both input qubits, then U<sub>f</sub>. Write the final state.
Let n = 2 and f(x) = 1 for every x. Write the state after kickback from input |00⟩|−⟩ and explain why no measurement on the input register can tell you that f is constant.
quiz.a: All signs are −1, so the state is −(1/2)(|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)|−⟩. The minus is global and unobservable; the input register is still uniform, so all four outcomes have probability 1/4, the same as for non-constant f. Separating the cases needs interference, for example a second Hadamard layer, as in 4.2.

beyond: Not for the exam. On real hardware the oracle is a compiled circuit, not a black box, and its cost in two-qubit and T gates decides whether phase kickback buys anything. SDKs such as Qiskit let you write a phase oracle directly, with the ancilla already in |−⟩, which is how Grover's diffuser is built. The same structure underlies qubitization and quantum signal processing, standard routes to simulating molecules and materials.
